almost, type. — case study 01 View live ↗
Educational product · End-to-end

Almost, Type.

Typography, one swipe at a time.

Gen Z will doomscroll for two hours without blinking. So I stopped fighting the scroll and built something worth scrolling — a typography app that teaches you one card at a time, in the browser, with no login.

no login mobile browser ~87 kB shipped one-handed WCAG 2.1 AA
Role
End-to-end — research, IA, visual design, front-end build & deploy
Timeline
4 weeks · solo · 2026
Type
Mobile-first PWA, runs in the browser
Tools
Figma · Claude · React · Tailwind · Vercel
01 · Problem

People make type decisions every day. Nobody taught them how.

Junior designers and developers choose fonts, sizes, and spacing constantly — on instinct, with no mental model behind it. The gap between “I know a font when I see it” and “I know why this font, at this size, on this background” is enormous, and almost nothing fills the middle.

Problem 01

Under-taught, or taught wrong

Design school gives type one chapter. Bootcamps skip it. YouTube cherry-picks a topic and never builds on it — leaving confident designers with fragile instincts.

Problem 02

Good resources are inaccessible

Butterick's is a masterpiece, but it's a book. Google Fonts shows thousands of typefaces without teaching when to use any of them. Workshops cost thousands.

Problem 03

Learning is a chore, not a habit

Design tools assume an hour of desk focus. Nobody built the “practise type for three minutes on your phone” experience — so people simply don't practise.

Where the idea came from My generation will scroll for two hours and remember nothing. The habit isn't the problem — the payload is. If the swipe is already muscle memory, why not put something useful under the thumb? That reframe became the product: don't ask people to study, hand them a better thing to scroll.
02 · Goals

Turn a subject people avoid into a habit they reach for

Interviews with recent design-adjacent grads surfaced one contradiction that shaped everything: everyone said they'd use a “Duolingo for typography.” Everyone said they wouldn't sign up for one.

Because users said
“I'd use it — but I'm not making an account.”
I designed
No login, no streaks, no notifications. Free, instant, disposable.
So that
Value lands in the first three seconds, on a phone, one-handed.

Ruled out: subscriptions, accounts, streak gamification, push notifications. Ruled in: free, no login, three-minute sessions, works offline after first load.

03 · Solutions

Four surfaces, one rule: useful before you decide to care

01 · Type School

Lessons you swipe, not lessons you study

Because nobody would sit through a course, lessons became a card stack: a memorable one-liner, a two-sentence why, and one actionable TRY THIS. Swipe right to save, left to skip.

The release runs on a spring-approximating cubic-bezier at 450 ms with ~12% overshoot — tuned until it felt like a native iOS card, with zero animation libraries. The harder problem was gesture arbitration: a six-pixel direction-lock dead zone lets the card own horizontal drag while the browser keeps vertical scroll, so long cards stay readable and neither gesture fights the other.

02 · Font Finder

Describe the vibe, get a shippable start

Because people froze at “thousands of fonts, which one?”, I replaced browsing with finding. Ten curated moods — “playful learning app”, “dark moody luxury” — each map to a pool of fonts and palettes.

You get four of each plus a live preview showing the fonts and colours working together, so the decision is made against a real layout instead of a specimen sheet. Refresh fonts, refresh palettes, or roll a new vibe — infinite non-repeating iterations.

03 · Colour Palette

Palettes split the way you'll actually use them

Three nice colours don't make an interface — knowing how much of each does. So every palette arrives distributed 60 · 30 · 10: background, UI surfaces, accent. Each swatch carries its hex and a plain-language role, which removes the guesswork between “pretty palette” and working screen.

04 · Library

Keep only what clicked

A swipe is worthless if the good card disappears. Everything you save lands in your Library — the lessons that actually landed stay one tap away, with notes and share built in. It's the quiet payoff that makes swiping feel like collecting instead of consuming.

04 · Research & Design

Three formats, two killed

  • A searchable textbook. Killed — nobody reads.
  • A daily newsletter. Killed — another email is another job.
  • A swipe deck. Kept — it borrows a motor pattern people already have and pays out in seconds.

Font Finder and the palette tool came straight out of interviews: people wanted help on real projects, not just abstract lessons. The visual identity took five passes to land on “Midnight Maison” — warm black, soft radial glow, and a burnt-orange TRY block that reads as a stamp, not a button. Everything runs on named colour tokens, so changing one token restyles the app.

I deployed the ugly first pass on day five to test on my actual phone in a coffee shop. Figma-good and thumb-good are different measurements — that loop drove every meaningful iteration after.

AI as a collaborator, not an author

I used Claude as a second designer — design critique on hierarchy, an accessibility review that caught my muted grey at a borderline 4.1:1 (fixed before ship), and Cowork to pair-program the front-end. Vision stayed mine; the distance from decision to shipped code went from days to hours. The lesson: ask for specifics, not solutions — “reduce the TRY glow to just the inner highlight” beats “make it better” — and verify every change on a real device.

05 · Reflection & Outcome

What the constraints taught me

Reflection 01

Constraints made the product

“No login” wasn't a compromise, it was the forcing function. Accounts would have meant onboarding, resets, verification — and a dead project by week two.

Reflection 02

Content is the design

A card lands because of the sentence, not the typeface. “Two fonts is a pairing. Three is a typo.” Writing the lessons was the design work.

Reflection 03

Meet the habit, don't fight it

Designing for how people already behave — thumb, feed, seconds — beat designing the app I thought they should want.

30+
micro-lessons
60+
fonts, 10 vibe bundles
4
surfaces, one system
~87 kB
shipped, gzipped

Usage analytics are being added via Vercel Analytics — I'd rather report real numbers here than claim ones I can't prove.

06 · Future Scope

Where it goes next

Next 01

Critique that reads the image

Move type critique from a self-rubric to real image analysis, flagging hierarchy and contrast straight from a screenshot.

Next 02

True physics + haptics

Swap the CSS spring approximation for real physics and add iOS haptic feedback, so the deck feels tactile as well as fast.

Next 03

The rubric as a free resource

Release the 8-point typography checklist as a downloadable cheat-sheet — useful standalone, and a reason to share the app.

Type — Apfel Grotezk by Collletttivo (SIL OFL) · Hanken Grotesk · Azeret Mono. Icons — Lucide.
Build — React 18 · Vite 5 · Tailwind CSS 3 · GitHub · Vercel. AI collaborator — Claude Cowork.

UX Research · IA · Product

Improving content discovery in educational streaming

Kanopy · Monash University

Students spent more time searching than learning. Kanopy is built like a film archive — but students arrive with academic intent and a mood, not a title in mind. I redesigned discovery so the right content surfaces in seconds instead of six minutes of scrolling.

3 screens redesigned 6 student interviews mood-led IA peer social proof
Role
UX research, information architecture, interaction & visual design
Timeline
5 weeks · 2026
Context
University-licensed streaming platform
Tools
Figma · paper wireframes · moderated testing
01 · Problem

Students spent more time searching than learning

Kanopy gives Monash students free access to thousands of documentaries and films. But the platform is organised the way a library catalogue is organised — by collection, festival, and faculty — while students arrive with something much fuzzier: an assignment, a mood, and forty minutes.

The result is friction at exactly the wrong moment. Students opened the app knowing roughly what they needed, then bounced between Browse → collections → search → back without a reliable way to judge whether anything was worth their time. Many gave up and went to YouTube.

Pain 01

Browsing beats intent

The home screen leads with curated shelves — Cannes, Criterion, Faculty Picks. None of it maps to “I need something on climate policy tonight.”

Pain 02

No signal of relevance

Every title looks equally plausible. Nothing tells a student whether this is the 40-minute doc their cohort found useful, or a three-hour art film.

Pain 03

Judgement costs a page load

Deciding on a title meant opening it, reading a synopsis, going back. Comparison across options was effectively impossible.

02 · Research

What students actually said

I ran moderated sessions with six Monash students, each given a realistic task — “find something worth watching for your unit this week” — plus a heuristic pass over the existing flows. Three insights repeated so consistently they became the design brief.

Insight 01
Students don't search by title, they search by state of mind — “something inspiring”, “I'm tired”, “I need to think deeply”.
Insight 02
The most trusted recommendation is a peer's. “If people in my unit watched it, it's probably relevant.”
Insight 03
Nobody reads a synopsis to decide. They want a one-line human reaction and a rating, fast.

How might we…

  • …let students start from a mood or intent instead of a collection name?
  • …make peer behaviour visible so relevance is obvious before opening a title?
  • …let someone compare options without leaving the screen?

Sketching the structure first

Before touching Figma I worked the information architecture on paper — cheap to throw away, and it kept me arguing about hierarchy instead of styling. The swipeable card stack for comparing picks came out of these sketches.

03 · Solutions

Three decisions, each traced back to an insight

Decision 01 · Home

Ask for a mood, not a category

Because students described what they wanted by state of mind rather than genre, I replaced the collection-led home with a single question — “What are you in mood to watch today?” — and a row of intent chips: Inspiring, Soft cry, Think deeply, Tired, Laugh, Brain rot mode, Comfort rewatch.

So that the first tap already narrows thousands of titles to a handful, with no search query and no vocabulary to learn. I deliberately did not add more navigation — the fix was giving the existing content a more human entry point.

Decision 02 · Curated picks

Make peer proof the headline, and let people compare by swiping

Because peer behaviour was the most trusted signal and comparison required page loads, I designed a swipeable stack where each pick leads with “18 students at Monash recommend this”, a peer score, and the IMDb rating side by side — plus one real reaction line instead of a synopsis.

So that a student can judge and compare three or four options in a few seconds of thumb movement, never leaving the screen. Relevance moved from something you discover after opening a title to something visible before you commit.

Decision 03 · Title detail

Answer “is this worth my time?” above the fold

Because students judged titles on human reaction rather than description, I restructured the detail page around a clear primary action and an About / Reviews split that defaults to peer reviews — each tagged with a feeling (“Uplifting”, “mind-bending”) and the reviewer's university.

So that runtime, rating, and social proof all land before any scrolling, and the decision takes one screen instead of three.

04 · Before & After

Three screens redesigned — every change tied to an insight

The originals aren't badly made; they're built for a different user. A film archive rewards browsing. A student on a deadline needs intent, relevance, and a fast decision. That's the shift these three screens make.

05 · Reflection & Outcome

What testing the prototype showed

I re-ran the original task — “find something worth watching for your unit this week” — with the same six participants on the new prototype, timing each attempt and asking for a confidence rating afterwards.

6:10 → 1:40
median time to choose a title
−73%
taps to reach a decision
5 / 6
participants completed unaided (was 2 / 6)
4.5 / 5
confidence in their pick (was 2.3)

These figures come from my own moderated prototype testing with six participants — a directional signal, not production analytics. I'd want a larger sample and real platform data before treating them as proven.

What I'd change

Reflection 01

Mood labels need testing, not taste

“Brain rot mode” tested as delightful with students and risky with staff. Playful labels are a real trade-off between resonance and institutional tone — worth validating, not assuming.

Reflection 02

Social proof has a cold-start problem

Peer counts are the strongest signal in the design and the first thing to break on a quiet campus. A fallback hierarchy — cohort, then faculty, then global — needs designing.

Reflection 03

I nearly added navigation

My first instinct was more filters and a bigger search. Research said the opposite: students didn't need more ways in, they needed the right one. Restraint was the actual design decision.

06 · Future Scope

Where it goes next

Next 01

Unit-aware recommendations

Connect to enrolment data so “your campus buzz” becomes “your unit's reading week” — relevance from the actual curriculum, not just the campus.

Next 02

Accessibility pass on the stack

The swipe needs a full keyboard and screen-reader equivalent, plus a reduced-motion path. A gesture-only comparison model excludes people.

Next 03

Validate at scale

Move from six moderated sessions to an instrumented A/B test on time-to-first-play, so the numbers above become real evidence.

Behaviour change · Sustainability

Making food waste visible enough to change

WasteLess — what's left matters.

Households waste ~30% more than they estimate — because it leaves a handful at a time. The hard part was never the maths. It was catching people before the bin.

2×
more scraps seen as usable after one session
<30s
from opening the app to a viable recipe
4.6/5
"I'd use this in my kitchen"
6 wks
solo, concept to tested prototype
Role
Research, behavioural strategy, IA, UI
Timeline
6 weeks · solo · 2026
Method
Design thinking · diary study · concept testing
Tools
Figma
01 · Problem

Waste is invisible until it's already expensive

I asked people to guess their weekly food waste, then photograph what they actually binned. Almost everyone under-estimated. Not carelessness — invisibility. Waste leaves in handfuls, and handfuls don't register as an amount.

Barrier 01

Feedback arrives too late

The decision to bin something takes seconds. A weekly report lands long after the behaviour it was meant to change.

Barrier 02

Abstract stats don't move anyone

"Food waste is 8% of global emissions" is useless at 7pm on a Tuesday. People need their number, in units they care about.

Barrier 03

Guilt burns out

Shame produces a spike, then abandonment. A habit needs a reason to return that feels good, not corrective.

The reframe I stopped designing a calculator and started designing a feedback loop — intercept the moment before the bin, and make reusing the easiest option in the room.
02 · Solutions

Four decisions, each tied to a barrier

01 · Capture in seconds

Point a camera at the mess instead of logging it

Manual logging is the step every food-waste app dies on. Scanning identifies scraps on the board and confirms them as chips — 3 items spotted, one tap. The explicit fallback ("Camera not cooperating? Type ingredients instead") matters more than the camera: a failure at step one loses the user permanently.

02 · Make the good choice the easy one

Rank by least waste, not most popular

Good intentions collapse when they cost extra effort. Results sort by Least waste by default, each showing what it uses and what it leaves — 5/5 ingredients, zero waste versus ~70g scraps. The app never asks for sacrifice; it reorders the menu.

03 · Feedback at the decision

Put the consequence next to the choice

Every recipe carries its own eco score and a scrap-impact meter — 230g, plotted low to high — plus one doable nudge: "Cut waste by 40%: simmer the peels into stock while the pasta cooks." Advice attached to the moment it's actionable, asking for an adjustment rather than a lifestyle.

04 · Make the month legible

Count what was rescued, never what was lost

The invisible finally adds up: 1.95kg rescued of a 3kg goal, 3.9kg CO₂ avoided, 14 meals cooked, $26 kept. Badges follow the same rule — earned ones celebrate, locked ones show the exact requirement. Nothing on screen reads as failure, only as rescued or not yet.

03 · Process

What I killed, and what testing broke

  • Weekly waste report — cut. Same after-the-fact trap as every competitor.
  • Household leaderboards — cut. Competition punishes whoever cooks most.
  • Manual weight logging — cut. Accurate, and nobody does it twice.
  • Scan → recipe → impact — kept. The only loop that closes inside one cooking session.
Testing killed v1
My first dashboard showed waste generated. Testers read it as a scoreboard of their failures.
The fix
Flip it to waste rescued. Identical maths.
The result
Testers went from avoiding the screen to wanting to open it again.

Onboarding failed the same way — it opened with climate statistics and testers glazed over. It now leads with what the app does for you, and the climate framing arrives second.

04 · Reflection & Next

What I'd change

Learned

Framing was the design

Generated vs rescued is the same number. One made people avoid the screen, the other made them return. My highest-impact decision was a word, not a layout.

Got wrong

I over-trusted the camera

Scanning demos beautifully and fails constantly on messy scraps in bad kitchen light. The typed fallback should have been an equal path from day one, not an edge case.

Next

Prove it properly

Predict spoilage before it happens, design for shared households, and run a longitudinal study against real bin weight — behaviour change only counts if it survives month three.

Numbers above are directional findings from my own concept testing with a small group — not production analytics. This is a design-thinking project, not a shipped product.

WasteLess — a self-directed design thinking project. Photography used for prototype illustration only.
